[Kushel et al. (2001)](https://doi.org/10.2105/AJPH.92.5.778)
conducted interviews with
"2578 homeless and marginally housed persons"
to determine risk factors for emergency department use.
Suppose they obtained the following results from a logistic regression analysis.

```
Call:
glm(formula = ED ~ age_transformed + crime_victim, family = binomial, 
    data = d)

Coefficients:
                  Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)   
(Intercept)       ????????????????????????????????????
age_transformed   -0.17435    0.07483   -2.33  0.00990 **   
crime_victim       0.80648    0.31259    2.58  0.00494 **
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
```

This is what the variables mean:

- `ED` is a 1 if the interviewee visited the emergency department
in the last twelve months and a 0 otherwise.
- If $a$ is the interviewee's age in years then
$$
\texttt{age\_transformed} = \frac{a - 40}{10} \text{.}
$$
- `crime_victim` is a 1 if the interviewee was the victim of a crime
in the last twelve months and a 0 otherwise.

Please answer the following questions.

## Problem 1

(1 point)
If the `Estimate` of the `(Intercept)` is $-4.60517$,
what are the odds of emergency department use for someone who is 50 years old
and was not the victim of a crime in the last twelve months?


(a) $\exp(-4.60517) \times \exp(-0.17435)$
(b) $\exp(-4.60517) \times \exp(5 \times -0.17435)$
(c) $\exp(-4.60517) \times \exp(10\times -0.17435)$
(d) $\exp(-4.60517) \times \exp(50\times -0.17435)$


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

(a)

If they're 50, their value for `age_transformed` would be $\displaystyle \frac{50 - 40}{10} = 1$.
If they weren't a victim of a crime then their value for `crime_victim` would be 0.
So, their odds would be $\exp(-4.60517-0.17435) = \exp(-4.60517) \times \exp(-0.17435)$.

:::


## Problem 2

(1 point)
If the `Estimate` of the `(Intercept)` is $-2.302585$,
what are the odds of emergency department use for someone who is 40 years old
and was the victim of a crime in the last twelve months?



(a) $\exp(-2.302585)$
(b) $\exp(-0.17435) \times \exp(-0.17435)$
(c) $\exp(-2.302585 + 0.80648)$
(d) $\exp(-2.302585 \times 0.80648)$


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

(c)

:::

## Problem 3

(1 point)
If the `Estimate` of the `(Intercept)` is $-0.80648$,
what are the odds of emergency department use for someone who is 40 years old
and was the victim of a crime in the last twelve months?


(a) 0
(b) 1/2
(c) 1
(d) $e$


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

(c)

:::

## Problem 4

(1 point)
We would expect the odds of emergency department use to increase
as age increases, holding crime victim status constant.


(a) This statement is true.
(b) This statement is false.
(c) Without additional information, it is impossible to know
if this statement is true or false.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

(b)

:::

## Problem 5

(1 point)
The odds of emergency department use are approximately 20% lower
among people who were a victim of a crime in the last twelve months
than among people who were not a victim of a crime in the last twelve months,
holding age constant.


(a) This statement is true.
(b) This statement is false.
(c) Without additional information, it is impossible to know
if this statement is true or false.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

(b)

:::



## Problem 6


(1 point)
The chance of emergency department use among people who are 40 years old
is less than 5%.


(a) This statement is true.
(b) This statement is false.
(c) Without additional information, it is impossible to know
if this statement is true or false.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

(c)

:::

## Problem 7

(1 point)
There is a statistically significant difference in the odds of emergency department use
between people who were the victim of a crime in the last twelve months
and people who were not, holding age constant.


(a) This statement is true.
(b) This statement is false.
(c) Without additional information, it is impossible to know
if this statement is true or false.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

(a)

:::



## Problem 8

(1 point)
Suppose we use this model to predict emergency department use for a new group of people,
sampled from the same population as the original group.
Those predictions have a very high sensitivity.
This means:

(a) A high proportion of people who are predicted to use the emergency room
end up using the emergency room.
(b) A high proportion of people who end up using the emergency room
are predicted to use the emergency room.
(c) A randomly-selected person who ends up using the emergency room
is very likely to have a higher fitted value than a randomly-selected person
who does not end up using the emergency room.
(d) There is a very low number of false positives.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

(b)

:::

## Problem 9

(1 point)
For this example, a well-calibrated model would, by definition, have:


(a) An even spread of fitted values between 0 and 1.
(b) High sensitivity and specificity.
(c) A high area under the curve.
(d) Fitted values that are close to the true probabilities of emergency department use.


::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

(d)

:::
